question: Follow-up to our previous questions on West Papua and the negotiations for the EU– Indonesia free trade agreement

In response to our previous questions (Written Questions E-005382/20211 and E-003902/20222) on the West Papua issue and the opportuneness of addressing it during negotiations for the EU– Indonesia free trade agreement (FTA), the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (VP/HR) stated: ‘The human rights situation in Indonesia is discussed in the context of the regular EU-Indonesia dialogue, which provides the most appropriate forum for a two-way in-depth exchange of views on all human rights, fundamental rights and related issues in the EU and Indonesia.

The EU is keen on scheduling the next dialogue, as soon as possible in 2023’3. Upon reviewing the 15th4 and 16th5 rounds of negotiations for this FTA, we noticed that human rights were not discussed, not even in the chapter for trade in sustainable development, the area in FTAs that covers labour, environmental, social and political rights. 1.

In light of this absence, do the VP/HR and the Commission negotiators encounter resistance from their Indonesian counterparts when they raise the issue of human rights, particularly with regard to West Papua?
Is Indonesia’s full respect for human rights, particularly with regard to West Papua, a red line for the EU when completing this FTA?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.3.2024) Human rights matters are mainstreamed into all policies of the EU. The Partnership and Cooperation Agreement1 sets the framework for the overall EU-Indonesia relationship, including trade relations, and establishes the respect for human rights as an essential underlying element.

The main dedicated channel to discuss human rights with Indonesia is the bilateral Human Rights Dialogue, not the negotiations on the EU-Indonesia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA). The CEPA negotiations aim at achieving an ambitious and comprehensive agreement, leading to increased trade and investment flows between the EU and Indonesia and contributing to sustainable development.

The last round of negotiations took place in the week of 26 February 2024 in Bandung, and talks were held in a constructive spirit. The EU eagerly awaits the next edition of the Human Rights Dialogue, to be scheduled in 2024. The EU’s objective is to ensure a constructive two-way discussion, during which Indonesian questions should be answered comprehensively.
